implementation_notes: SwiftData realizes the pattern declaratively: the child is a @Model class held in a @Relationship on the parent with deleteRule: .cascade, and the ModelContext inserts, updates and saves it together with the parent - the child is never fetched or saved through its own context. Declare the inverse relationship so the object graph stays consistent, and keep the child type out of any query of its own. This requires iOS 17/macOS 14; older deployment targets use Core Data's cascade delete rule instead.
pitfalls: Deleting the parent cascades to the child, so the same object must never be referenced by a second parent - a shared row would be deleted with either one (declare the inverse to avoid duplicate object graphs).
Saving a child on its own has no persistent effect: mutations are only stored when the context saves the parent's graph.

variants.name: Core Data relationship with cascade delete rule
variants.implementation_notes: In Core Data the dependent mapping is a to-many relationship whose delete rule is cascadeDeleteRule: deleting the owning managed object deletes the referenced children, and the children are fetched through the parent relationship (relationshipKeyPathsForPrefetching) rather than with their own fetch requests. It is the same contract as SwiftData's cascade relationship with much older deployment targets; prefer SwiftData on new projects unless Core Data's tooling is required.
variants.code_sketch:
let req = NSFetchRequest<NSManagedObject>(entityName: "Order")
req.relationshipKeyPathsForPrefetching = ["lines"]        // children via parent
let entity = NSEntityDescription.entity(forEntityName: "Order", in: ctx)!
entity.relationshipsByName["lines"]!.deleteRule = .cascadeDeleteRule
pitfalls: A cascade rule deletes every object reachable through the relationship - a child referenced from elsewhere silently disappears.
Bulk deletes (NSBatchDeleteRequest) operate below the object graph and do not apply relationship delete rules, so they can leave orphans.
